chapter: Dance jobs and the opera house
title: The Japanese Tea Garden at Milneburg and Moreau's camp
summary: He describes the tea garden's lakeside location, the Smoky Mary train, and playing at Moreau's camp in 1928 with Sidney Miner, his brother and others, often playing late and into breakfast dances.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: What was that Japanese tea garden like? Was it over the water, out in the camp?

Well, it was right by the water. The Japanese tea garden set right, no, right at the, right by the lake, you see. And then, well, you had to go on the run, or the walkway to get to the camp. It was not on the camp, it was, you know, right on land, but right at the foot of the lake.
Where the railroad went out through, the Spokin Mary?

Close to the camp, close to it. On the side of the baudouin? Yeah, no, Spokin Mary didn't come all the way in front of the Japanese Tea Garden. They had a little, it comes about where Moreau's Grocery is right now. Yeah, I know. And the grocery's there right now. Me and Sidney Miner, you and my brother, and the band, Joe Cliff, I never, Reuben McClendon, McClendon, that he's away from the Southern Moccan Company right now. Well, we were playing at Moreau's Camp in 1928, at Lilwood's. And Moreau's got the same grocery there now. He's still at the same grocery there. Yeah. I wonder if it is still there. I don't know if the grocery's there, but I think the family's still there. We'll take a ride at that, see, sometime, you know. Yeah, I think it may still be there. You know what we said last night? Well, if the place is torn down, it's torn down recently, because I passed there, I guess, six or eight months ago, I would say, or maybe longer. And I look at that place, I say, oh, Moreau, you know, to myself, like that. They just have a very, a pretty good saxophone player. There's a player next door at a place called Baradice, next to the Japanese T-Guard. Boy, I've heard of that. His name was Hickman. And sometime I say, I say, sometime I'm going to play like that, man. But I don't know what happened. Eleven o'clock every night, they was closing up. We'd be there at three or four o'clock in the morning, and then Bob Wachers would say sometime, look, y'all want to play a little breakfast dance or picnic or something? He'd say, yeah. I'd call, get on the phone and call my mother and tell her, we have to play a breakfast dance or something, and he'd come in town and get some of his friends to come on back out there and we'd be playing until 10, 11, 12 o'clock in the day. So I don't know what happened. That's why I always believe a man should play a little melody. Some, let people know they're playing. That's what's the cause of that. That place we throw some nice 11, 12 o'clock. Everybody, probably next door could hear what I was playing on the saxophone. But not taking nothing away from him, it was pretty good.
